title: Using ChatGPT for Science Learning: A Study on Pre-service Teachers' Lesson Planning
extended_summary:
This preprint examines how pre-service teachers envision using ChatGPT in science education, addressing the lack of empirical work on the practical integration of large language models into classroom teaching and learning. The study asks three questions: what range of science content and instructional strategies can be combined with ChatGPT in lesson plans, how proficient pre-service teachers are in planning such integration, and what usefulness and concerns they perceive regarding ChatGPT in science learning.

The intervention consisted of a short instructional sequence in which 29 pre-service elementary teachers at a Korean teachers' university participated in four weekly 2-hour sessions. These sessions introduced ChatGPT, discussed its possible benefits for science education, reviewed science teaching methods, and guided participants in writing a 45-minute elementary science lesson plan that incorporated ChatGPT. Data included the lesson plans, simulated ChatGPT conversations attached to the plans, rubric-based evaluations using a modified TPACK/TIAR instrument, and open-ended survey responses. The analysis combined descriptive quantitative scoring with qualitative coding of perceptions and concerns.

The population was mostly sophomore pre-service elementary science teachers in South Korea, enrolled in a "Science Education 1" course and having previously completed a 3-week on-site school training experience. The study was conducted in a classroom-based university course context rather than in actual K-12 implementation. Participants designed lesson plans spanning biology, chemistry, earth science, physics, and environmental science, and used a wide range of methods such as cooperative learning, POE, learning cycle, analogy generation, experimentation, and concept mapping.

The main conclusions are that pre-service teachers saw ChatGPT as broadly applicable across science domains and pedagogical strategies, and their lesson plans were rated relatively strong overall on the modified TPACK-based rubric (mean 3.29/4). They were strongest in aligning ChatGPT with instructional strategies and somewhat weaker in selecting ChatGPT functions appropriately. Qualitative findings showed that participants anticipated benefits such as high-quality questioning, self-directed and individualized learning, and formative assessment, while also expressing concerns about inaccuracy, hallucinations, bias, and student overdependence. The authors argue that more research is needed in real classroom settings and that teacher preparation should include AI literacy and guidance on appropriate instructional use of LLMs.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: An OpenAI large language model chatbot used for natural-language question answering, content support, and interactive dialogue.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as the tool pre-service elementary teachers integrated into science lesson plans for a 45-minute class; the paper analyzed intended uses across science domains, evaluated lesson plans with a modified TPACK/TIAR rubric, and captured teachers' perceived benefits and concerns.

findings.finding_summary: Across 29 pre-service elementary teachers' science lesson plans, ChatGPT integration was rated relatively high on a modified TPACK-based rubric, with an overall mean of M = 3.29 (SD = .91) on a 1–4 scale. Subscores were M = 3.44 (SD = .87) for 'curriculum goals & ChatGPT,' M = 3.48 (SD = .99) for 'instructional strategies & ChatGPT,' M = 3.00 (SD = .93) for 'ChatGPT function selection(s),' and M = 3.24 (SD = .83) for 'fit,' indicating stronger lesson-strategy integration than functional exploitation of ChatGPT.
findings.measure: Modified TPACK-based Technology Integration Assessment Rubric (TIAR) scores on lesson plans

findings.finding_summary: Pre-service teachers showed significantly higher performance in integrating ChatGPT into instructional strategies than in selecting appropriate ChatGPT functions. A paired-samples t-test found a significant difference between item 2 ('instructional strategies & ChatGPT,' M = 3.48, SD = .99) and item 3 ('ChatGPT function selection(s),' M = 3.00, SD = .93), t(28) = 2.3173, p = .0280.
findings.measure: Difference between TIAR subscale scores for instructional strategies vs. ChatGPT function selection

findings.finding_summary: Survey responses indicated that pre-service teachers perceived ChatGPT as supporting questioning, self-directed learning, individualized support, and formative assessment in science learning. Reported frequencies included knowledge construction through questioning (16/29), individualized learning support (9/29), formative evaluation/feedback (8/29), critical thinking support (5/29), and digital competency benefits (4/29).
findings.measure: Open-ended survey perceptions of usefulness and anticipated outcomes

findings.finding_summary: Pre-service teachers also reported concerns about ChatGPT's limitations and risks in science learning. Concerns included accuracy/reliability issues (11/29), possible misinformation or misconceptions, and student over-dependence on ChatGPT (13/29); the paper also documented inappropriate planned uses such as relying on non-existent YouTube links generated by ChatGPT and using it for visually dependent tasks like locating constellations.
findings.measure: Open-ended survey concerns and qualitative lesson-plan analysis of inappropriate use cases

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical mixed-methods study of 29 pre-service teachers' lesson plans and perceptions, but it does not test student learning outcomes in a randomized or quasi-experimental design. Evidence is based on rubric scores and qualitative survey responses about intended use rather than classroom impact.
impact_tier_rationale: The study reports promising perceptions and relatively high lesson-plan integration scores, but no direct effect on student achievement or classroom outcomes is measured. Impact is therefore suggestive but unclear.
